## From agricultural drainage to abandonment: the forgotten history

To understand what the Charca de Suárez represents today, it is worth going back to a time when water was not welcome in this corner of the Granada coastline. During the 1960s, the development fever sweeping through southern Spain found in the Motril marshes an obstacle to agricultural expansion. Those waterlogged lands, considered unhealthy and unproductive, were subjected to an ambitious drainage plan intended to gain fertile soil for sugarcane and vegetables. The dewatering pumps worked tirelessly to expel the water that had shaped the landscape for centuries. The message of the era was clear: wet land was wasted land.

The transformation was rapid and decisive. Drainage channels replaced the old lagoons, and plantations spread over what had once been the domain of reeds and waterfowl. Sugarcane, the region's star crop, found in these soils what appeared to be ideal ground to thrive. Vegetables completed an agricultural mosaic that promised profitability and employment for a population that lived mainly off the land. No one seemed to notice then the ecological value of that wetland disappearing beneath the plow. Biodiversity did not feature among the priorities of a Spain seeking to modernize at any cost.

The mirage lasted barely two decades. By the mid-1980s, the crisis in the sugar sector and changes in European Community agricultural policy undermined the profitability of those crops. The farms began to be abandoned one after another, leaving behind a degraded and ownerless landscape. The drainage channels became clogged with sediment, the hydraulic infrastructure deteriorated, and the land was left exposed to erosion. Agricultural abandonment turned the area into a salty wasteland where only a few ruderal species grew. It was a period of silence and oblivion that, paradoxically, prepared the ground for an unexpected recovery.

Nature, however, had not given up on that corner. Groundwater seepage, fed by the aquifer of the Motril plain, began to surface in the depressions of the abandoned land. The rains did the rest, accumulating in the old agricultural plots and forming seasonal ponds. The water was returning to its place, this time without planning or human intervention. The first to notice were the neighbors of the adjoining farms, who watched with curiosity as the low-lying areas flooded every winter and remained wet well into spring.

Those incipient ponds acted as a magnet for wildlife. Waterfowl, always attentive to habitat availability, began to arrive in search of shelter and food. First came the most common species: mallards, coots, and moorhens that found in the shallow waters a safe place to breed. Then came the waders, attracted by the mudflats rich in invertebrates. Local naturalists, accustomed to touring the Granada coast in search of interesting observations, began to take notice of that enclave that appeared on no map of natural areas. Their field notebooks filled with records pointing to something more than a simple seasonal puddle.

The systematic documentation of these observations proved decisive. During the early 1990s, a group of birdwatching enthusiasts and residents concerned about the environmental deterioration of the area began compiling data on the species present in the old marshes. Their lists included migratory birds that used the wetland as a stopover on their routes between Europe and Africa, as well as threatened species that found in those ponds a refuge increasingly scarce on the Mediterranean coast. The evidence was compelling: the wetland that had been drained for being considered unproductive was demonstrating an ecological value no one had foreseen.

Those records drove the first formal demands for protection. The naturalists and residents involved in monitoring the area presented their data to local and regional authorities, calling for recognition of the site's value and for measures to ensure its conservation. It was not an easy path. The land, fragmented across multiple private properties, presented considerable legal complexity. Moreover, the social image of the area remained associated with abandonment and degradation, making it difficult for institutions to see in those ponds a space worthy of protection.

The history of the Charca de Suárez is, in this sense, the chronicle of a double transformation. First came the systematic drainage of a wetland considered an obstacle to agricultural progress. Then came abandonment, degradation, and finally the spontaneous recovery of an ecosystem that refused to disappear. Between both moments, the silent work of those who documented the arrival of waterfowl proved fundamental in changing the social and political perception of the site. What in the 1960s was seen as an unhealthy terrain that should be drained, in the 1990s began to be viewed as a natural heritage deserving protection.

The process was neither linear nor free of tensions. The agricultural interests that still maintained activity in the area viewed with suspicion any protection initiative that might limit their uses. The owners of the abandoned plots, for their part, were not always willing to cede their land for conservation purposes. The local administration, pressured by both sides, moved cautiously through legally and socially complex terrain. Even so, the biological data accumulated during those years provided a solid basis for justifying public intervention. Citizen science, practiced by naturalists with no more resources than their binoculars and field notebooks, became the main argument for defending the wetland's recovery.

Today, as the Charca de Suárez consolidates itself as a benchmark for conservation on the Granada coast, it is worth remembering that none of this was written in advance. The wetland that now receives million-euro investments and attracts visitors from all over Andalusia was, for decades, a forgotten and degraded space. Its rebirth began with a phenomenon as simple as water once again rising from the earth, and was consolidated thanks to the perseverance of those who knew how to see in those ponds something more than wasteland. The history of its drainage and abandonment is, ultimately, the necessary prologue for understanding the value of what is now protected.
